items.title: The Peacock Flower and Reproductive Resistance Under Slavery
items.description:
European naturalists documented the peacock flower's medicinal uses but left its most consequential history behind.

The post The Peacock Flower and Reproductive Resistance Under Slavery appeared first on JSTOR Daily.
items.content:
Admired for their striking beauty, the fiery blossoms of the peacock flower have long captured the attention of people across the Atlantic world. Known today as Barbados Pride and Red Bird of Paradise, the tropical shrub was identified by eighteenth-century naturalists as flos pavonis or Poinciana pulcherrima L., a species now classified as Caesalpinia pulcherrima (L.) Sw. As economic botany expanded throughout the New World, European collectors sought plants with potential commercial, medicinal, and agricultural value. Among the species they transported from the Caribbean to Europe was the peacock flower, where it became a favored ornamental plant in botanical gardens.

These Europeans did not similarly preserve the knowledge held by Caribbean communities about the plant’s medicinal uses. Enslaved women across the Caribbean possessed knowledge of the peacock flower’s medicinal properties and used it as an abortifacient, a substance that could be used to induce menstruation or facilitate abortion. For these women, using the peacock flower was one way to exercise control over their reproductive capacities within a racial capitalist system that commodified their fertility and viewed the birth of children as an expansion of enslaved property.

In the context of the peacock flower, European scientific communities “chose to remain ignorant of West Indian abortifacients.”

Historian of science Londa Schiebinger has used the history of the peacock flower to examine the unequal movement of botanical knowledge across the Atlantic world. European observers in Suriname, Jamaica, Saint-Domingue (modern-day Haiti), and Barbados recorded how enslaved and Indigenous women used the plant to induce abortion or menstruation. Although European naturalists encountered and documented its use as an abortifacient across the Caribbean, this knowledge was not incorporated into European medical and botanical traditions. The peacock flower’s history reveals that colonial science involved more than simply collecting and transferring knowledge. According to Schiebinger, it also operated as a process of selection and cultivation, through which some forms of knowledge were preserved and circulated while others were excluded from the bounds of recognized science.

One of the most significant European accounts of this knowledge came from Maria Sibylla Merian, a German naturalist and scientific illustrator who traveled to Suriname with her daughter in 1699 on a scientific expedition. In her 1705 work Metamorphosis insectorum Surinamensium, or Metamorphosis of the Insects of Suriname, Merian documented the peacock flower alongside the insects and plants she studied in the Dutch colony. Notably, her account of the plant drew on testimony from enslaved African and Indigenous women who told her they used the plant’s seeds to prevent their children from being born into slavery. In the chapter “Lost Knowledge, Bodies of Ignorance, and the Poverty of Taxonomy as Illustrated by the Curious Fate of Flos Pavonis, an Abortifacient,” Schiebinger reproduces Merian’s account:

The Indians, who are not treated well by their Dutch masters, use the seeds [of this plant] to abort their children, so that their children will not become slaves like they are. The black slaves from Guinea and Angola have demanded to be well treated, threatening to refuse to have children. In fact, they sometimes take their own lives because they are treated so badly, and because they believe they will be born again, free and living in their own land. They told me this themselves.

As Schiebinger argues in Plants and Empire: Colonial Bioprospecting in the Atlantic World, Merian’s account differed from those of other European observers because she “placed abortion squarely within the colonial struggle,” recognizing enslaved women’s use of the plant as a form of resistance to a system that sought to control their reproductive lives. Historian Jennifer Morgan similarly contends that enslaved women’s reproductive capacities were essential for the economic logic of hereditary racial slavery. She argues that the Black female body became a site of labor, reproduction, violence, and resistance, making fertility itself a domain of political struggle. In this context, the refusal to bear a child served both to “inflict damage on the regime” and to reject the “legitimacy of enslavement to begin with.”

More to Explore

A History Wrapped in Banana Leaves

Sophia Rey
May 28, 2026
How hallacas and the banana plant became intertwined in Venezuelan cultural memory.

Merian was not the first European naturalist to record the use of the peacock flower as an abortifacient. Ten years earlier, English physician and naturalist Sir Hans Sloane had documented the plant in Jamaica, where he described its ability to “[provoke] the Menstrua” and “[cause] Abortion.” Unlike Merian, Sloane framed the practice as evidence of women’s trickery, warning of deceptive women who secretly sought abortions from “unsuspecting doctors” rather than considering the conditions of bondage that shaped enslaved women’s reproductive choices. A similar account emerged in 1799 from Michel Descourtilz in Saint-Domingue, where the French physician and naturalist also recorded the peacock flower’s abortifacient use but interpreted it through the perspective of plantation authorities, condemning enslaved women for the “‘ill intentions’ of the ‘negresses’ who aborted their offspring.”

These accounts demonstrate that European naturalists did not lack access to knowledge about the peacock flower’s abortifacient properties. Rather, the absence of this knowledge in European botanical and medical traditions reflected the priorities of colonial science. In the context of the peacock flower, European scientific communities “chose to remain ignorant of West Indian abortifacients.” Schiebinger uses agnotology, a methodological approach that examines how ignorance is produced and maintained, to analyze the making of this scientific ignorance. As she argues, scientific inquiry was shaped by broader forces including “funding priorities, global strategies, national policies, the structures of scientific institutions, trade patterns, and gender politics,” which directed attention toward certain forms of knowledge while leaving others unexplored.

For Schiebinger, the suppression of knowledge about abortifacients reflected a form of “cultured apathy or cultivated indifference” toward reproductive knowledge that challenged political and economic priorities. In the eighteenth-century Atlantic world, European governments advanced pronatalist policies that celebrated population growth as a source of national power. Meanwhile, amid debates over the end of the transatlantic slave trade, enslaved women’s reproduction became increasingly important to plantation societies seeking to expand the population of enslaved people in accordance with impending trade restrictions. Thus, knowledge about limiting fertility conflicted with the interests of European states and plantation societies that valued population growth. As Schiebinger explains, “the same forces feeding the explosion of knowledge we associate with the Scientific Revolution and global expansion led to an implosion of knowledge of herbal abortifacients.” As a result, knowledge of the peacock flower’s abortifacient properties remained rooted in Caribbean communities rather than becoming incorporated into European botanical and medical traditions.

The history of the peacock flower reveals that botanical knowledge is inextricably linked to the social and political worlds in which it was produced. In the case of the peacock flower, the gaps in the scientific record expose as much as the knowledge it contains, demonstrating how systems of power and culturally produced ignorance influenced what was and was not preserved as scientific knowledge. The Plant Humanities Initiative at Dumbarton Oaks seeks to explore histories like this one, illuminating the many ways that plants and people have shaped each other across time and place.

items.title: How a Murder Fueled Racial Terror in Florida
items.description:
The hunt for Charlie Wright exposed how convict leasing, labor tensions, and white supremacy shaped rural life in the Jim Crow South.

The post How a Murder Fueled Racial Terror in Florida appeared first on JSTOR Daily.
items.content:
On December 2, 1922, the grisly remains of a white, 24-year-old high school teacher named Ruby Hendry were found in tall grass beside a train track in the town of Perry, Florida. As historian Christopher Calton writes, the manhunt that followed was also a campaign of terror shaped by economic and social forces that affected rural Florida in the years after World War I.

Perry is the seat of Taylor County, a part of northern Florida long known for being hostile to Black people. But, in 1913, the owners of a new sawmill began bringing in skilled workers from Louisiana, some of them Black, nearly tripling the Black population of the town.

After being brought to a turpentine camp through the convict leasing system, men were often kept there through debt peonage, which could change a three-month sentence into a lifetime of enslavement.

Laura Scott Reaves, who was a child at the time of the manhunt, told Calton that white men in Perry, facing their own hardships due to the economic downturn following the end of the war, were furious at the hiring of Black foremen. They began a campaign of terrorism that drove many of them to flee north.

The day after Hendry’s body was discovered, police arrested four local Black men as suspects despite having found no meaningful clues. A few days later, they announced that the murder had apparently been committed by a man named Charlie Wright, an “escaped convict” from nearby Dixie County.

Calton writes that the label of escaped convict carried a very specific meaning—a Black man forced by the convict leasing system into hard labor at an isolated turpentine camp deep in the forest. Dixie County had been incorporated just the previous year on a nearly uninhabited area owned by the Putnam Lumber Company. By making it a county, the company created a jurisdiction with a local court that funneled incarcerated people into lumber and turpentine camps.

More to Explore

Remembering the Rosewood Massacre

Edward González-Tennant
January 1, 2023
On January 1, 1923, Rosewood, Florida, was a thriving town of mostly African American residents. Seven days later, it was gone, burned to the ground by a white mob.

Police might arrest a man at random on the street, extort him for money, and, if he was unable to pay, charge him with vagrancy. After being brought to a turpentine camp through the convict leasing system, men were often kept there through debt peonage, which could change a three-month sentence into a lifetime of enslavement.

Calton writes that although no evidence was ever publicly released linking Wright to Hendry’s murder, hundreds of white men, assisted by tracking hounds, surrounded the swamp where he was hiding. Vigilantes also menaced the homes of Black Perry residents who they claimed might give him refuge and killed a number of Black residents, reportedly including children. The mob burned the community’s church, school, Masonic lodge, and amusement hall—one building each night that Wright remained on the loose.

“It is impossible to identify how much of the violence stemmed from a culture of racism and notions of honor and how much, if any, was motivated by labor tensions in a depressed economy,” Calton writes.

After six days on the run, Wright was finally captured. A mob of thousands, from across northern Florida and southern Georgia, chained him to a wooden stake, placed dried grass doused in turpentine on the ground, and set him on fire. The episode illustrates how systems of racial oppression and forced labor reinforced one another in the Jim Crow South.

items.title: Why the Washington Monument Looks the Way It Does
items.description:
For nearly a century, Americans argued over how to honor George Washington. The monument they built reflected those debates.

The post Why the Washington Monument Looks the Way It Does appeared first on JSTOR Daily.
items.content:
The Washington Monument towers above the nation’s capital at nearly 555 feet. Between 1884 and 1889, it was the tallest structure in the world. Art and architecture historian Kirk Savage writes that the monument “both overpowers and empowers, first diminishing the visitor into insignificance and then raising him skyward like a hero.”

The monument’s history is tangled. Savage continues, “The undertaking began in the eighteenth century …, ran into partisan warfare after [George Washington’s] death, and foundered for decades in unending disputes over designs and intentions.” Conflicts over monuments, it turns out, are not exclusive to the twenty-first century.

“Necessity made Washington an instant icon, and from the beginning necessity buried the real figure beneath a mound of verse, oratory, and imagery.”

The problem was that the nation couldn’t decide what to do, what to think, about George Washington himself. And that, argues Savage, was wrapped up in “long-standing disputes over national identity.” Washington and his monument were “symbolic battlegrounds” over the nature of leadership in a republic, over the contradiction of a first citizen.

“Necessity made Washington an instant icon, and from the beginning necessity buried the real figure beneath a mound of verse, oratory, and imagery, all vying to give shape to the icon and therefore the nation.”

How then to portray an icon? The American Revolution was the first of many “no kings” protests, yet the Continental Congress’s initial effort to honor Washington in 1783 called for an equestrian statue on the model of imperial Rome (Marcus Aurelius) and Bourbon France (Louis XV). Federalists were for this grand gesture, but their opponents, Jeffersonian republicans (later called Democrat-Republicans), were against such monarchical trappings. Yet in 1791, they agreed to name the new federal capital Washington, District of Columbia.

More to Explore

The First Civil Rights Monument

Matthew Wills
February 19, 2018
The nation's first civil rights monument is a mural portraying the interracial audience at Marion Anderson's famed Freedom Concert of 1939 on the Washington Mall.

Upon Washington’s death in 1799, the factions agreed that he should be buried in his eponymous capital city, despite his instructions that he be buried at Mount Vernon. But they could not come up with a consensus for the type of tomb. In early 1801, Federalists in Congress passed a scheme for a pyramid-shaped mausoleum, but newly inaugurated President Thomas Jefferson shelved the proposal. Washington stayed buried in Mount Vernon.

With the national government endlessly stymied over the issue, local Washingtonians stepped in to form the private Washington National Memorial Society in 1833. Belying its name, it was all D.C. players “active in promoting the unrealized city that was still a swampy backwater.” The Society’s George Watterston called for an obelisk that would be “the highest edifice in the world and the most stupendous and magnificent monument ever erected to man.”

Architect Robert Mills’ design, finally chosen by the Society in 1845, was almost exactly what Watterston envisioned. Mills’ plan included a 100-foot-high Doric colonnade around a flat-topped obelisk. Mills was reputed to have said that an unembellished shaft—which he would not live to see—would look like “a stalk of asparagus.”  

The Society solicited donations of money and stone from around the world and started work. Pope Pius IX chipped in with a slab of marble from the ruins of the Forum in 1855. This enraged nativist “Know-Nothings” of the American Party, convinced that Catholic immigrants from Ireland and Germany were plotting to take control of the US. Fired up by telegraph inventor Samuel Morse, they smashed the Pope’s gift and threw it into the Potomac. They also seized control of the Society itself, insisting that only “Americans” (meaning native-born Protestants) could fund a monument to Washington. Their three-year fund-raising campaign proved a bust, however, yielding a mere $51.66. 

So for twenty years the uncompleted stump of a tower looked, according to Mark Twain, like “a factory chimney with the top broken off.” After the Civil War, in Savage’s words, “the stump seemed to represent a nation that had lost its way.” When Congress refused to fund its completion in time for the 1876 Centennial, there were even demands that the eyesore be torn down. But then, during the Centennial year, Congress suddenly acted to fund and complete the tower.

“The nation could unify around Washington’s monument only after dismissing the question it had so insistently posed, the question of his legacy,” writes Savage. “Washington no longer mattered, not even in his own monument.”

Lieutenant Colonel Thomas Casey of the Army Corps of Engineers became the designer of the revived project. Instead of proposed neoclassical or Neo-Gothic towers, he continued on with the obelisk, but stripped it of all embellishment and added a pyramidion to the top. Inside, he put in the technological marvel of an elevator. (Pro tip: they didn’t add plumbing.) 

Elsewhere, Washington is portrayed astride a horse or atop a column; shirtless, in classical garb, or, more commonly, in a long coat and tricorn. At the national memorial to the man, however, he is nowhere to be found. Instead, as Savage observes, visitors ascend an empty obelisk and, for a moment, “take the place of the hero himself.”

items.title: Born Without a Country
items.description:
In Southeast Asia, colonial legacies and citizenship policies continue to leave hundreds of thousands without legal nationality.

The post Born Without a Country appeared first on JSTOR Daily.
items.content:
Because they aren’t recognized as citizens by any country, stateless people lack “the right to have rights,” as the political philosopher Hannah Arendt famously put it. Having fled Nazi Germany as a Jewish refugee in 1933, Arendt herself spent nearly two decades of her life stateless. Nearly a century later, statelessness persists as a problem all over the world—including in Southeast Asia, where hundreds of thousands may be affected.

Christoph Sperfeldt, a researcher who focuses on statelessness, explains that few Southeast Asian countries ratified the major international agreements adopted in 1954 and 1961. He notes recent progress, however: in 2012, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations declared that “every person has the right to a nationality as prescribed by law.”

Still, stateless populations are especially vulnerable to cross-border criminal cartels involved in human trafficking, gun-running, and drug smuggling, warns researcher Bill Berkeley.

The long history of colonialism in Southeast Asia is one reason statelessness persists in the region.

Sakinah Kahtu was being smuggled to Malaysia—a desperate act arranged by her parents to protect her from potential sexual violence by government soldiers—when her boat was seized by human traffickers, who demanded a high “asking price” for her freedom. A stranger who paid the ransom married her days later—even though Sakinah, an ethnic minority Rohingya unable to claim citizenship in Myanmar, may still have been a minor.

Her story “illustrates the often overlooked linkages between statelessness and early and forced marriage,” writes human rights lawyer Sheila Menz. “[B]ecause no state had conferred a nationality under which Kahtu could claim protection … she was forced to flee and rendered particularly vulnerable to exploitation, trafficking, and gender-based violence.”

The long history of colonialism in Southeast Asia is one reason statelessness persists in the region. “Many state-building projects were confined to borders drawn by colonial powers and have since witnessed a dynamic reformulation of citizenship regimes, often nurtured by intercommunal tensions that had been exacerbated during colonial rule,” Sperfeldt explains. For example, a grassroots organization in Malaysia found more than 12,350 undocumented individuals descended from Tamil Indians who migrated during the British colonial period.

Poor record-keeping can be another cause of statelessness, especially among ethnic minorities, refugees, and people living in remote communities, since children whose births aren’t registered are often unable to prove their parentage and claim nationality.

Sperfeldt points out that most stateless Southeast Asians belong to “minorities who live in the country in which they were born,” such as ethnic Vietnamese in Cambodia or ethnic Chinese in Brunei.

More to Explore

Asian South America

Matthew Wills
October 20, 2022
The migration of Asian people—from India, from China, from Japan—to South America and the Caribbean began as early as the sixteenth century.

“[L]aws may be well drafted but their application has consistently shown discriminatory patterns. An example is the difficulties faced by stateless Vietnamese populations in Cambodia in accessing birth registration, not to mention nationality,” he elaborates.

In 2018, a junior football team in Thailand made headlines for surviving nearly three weeks in a flooded cave complex—but their dramatic rescue also shone a spotlight on the plight of the team’s assistant coach and three of the 12 boys who were trapped.

The multilingual teenager who acted as an interpreter between the team and British rescue divers belongs to the Wa ethnic minority and was born stateless. He and his fellow stateless teammates received Thai citizenship after their rescue.

This predicament is not limited to the Wa, but also affects other regional indigenous and tribal groups, such as Karen and Hmong communities in the highlands of Thailand.

Many members of these hill tribes lack access to education, healthcare, legal employment, and suffrage, with Berkeley calling them “rightless”—a word straight from Arendt.

Get your fix of JSTOR Daily’s best stories in your inbox each Thursday.

Yet statelessness is often obscured when individuals with irregular paperwork—such as the Rohingya refugees fleeing Myanmar for Malaysia—are criminalized as “illegal migrants.”

Human rights law experts David Weissbrodt and Clay Collins observe that statelessness can be addressed through “preemptive remedies,” such as properly registering births and constitutionally granting citizenship to children who would otherwise be born stateless.

Still, for nation-states, naturalizing all residents who currently lack citizenship can be “the only complete remedy for stateless persons,” they add. The scholarship suggests that statelessness is less an administrative oversight than a consequence of the ways states define who belongs.

items.title: The Secret Lives of Insects
items.description:
Can fruit flies have dialects? Can dung beetles navigate by the stars? Find surprising answers in this collection of stories about bugs and people.

The post The Secret Lives of Insects appeared first on JSTOR Daily.
items.content:
Fruit flies that speak in different dialects. Arctic mites that can survive a deep freeze. Bees that “dance” to communicate. The insect world is stranger and far more fascinating than it first appears. In this roundup we’ve brought together stories of remarkable bugs, the people who study them, and the many ways insects have shaped human history, science, and culture.

How Insects Think

The Bee Dance Debate

Danny Robb
October 1, 2025
Can insects communicate? In the middle of the twentieth century, scientists disagreed on whether bees could possess a “language” expressed through motion.

New Study Finds Insects Speak in Different “Dialects”

Lina Zeldovich
July 31, 2018
Different fruit flies species can learn each other’s language to warn against parasitic wasps.

The Amazingly Complex World of Insect Navigation

James MacDonald
June 22, 2016
Dung beetles, ants, and other insects navigate in mysterious ways.

Are Insects Capable of Moral Behavior?

Livia Gershon
February 6, 2020
Some 19th-century naturalists believed that bugs could think and should therefore definitely know that biting is out of line.

Insects and Survival

How Do Insects Survive Winter?

Olivia Box
November 4, 2021
Some species have adapted to get themselves close to freezing without dying.

What Do We Lose When We Lose a Species?

Kevin Litman-Navarro
December 28, 2017
Debates about the moral value of biodiversity are longstanding in the world of environmental ethics, and the issue is far from settled.

Why Conservationists Shouldn’t Forget About Insects

James MacDonald
July 10, 2017
Insect conservation can be a tough sell. Lots of people simply don’t like bugs, and an endangered bug simply doesn’t pull on the heart strings.

Scientists Are Putting Mosquitoes on Human Diet Drugs

Lina Zeldovich
February 19, 2019
Humans and mosquitoes share a surprising amount of genes and have similar hunger controls.

Sting! (Don’t Stand So Close to the Tarantula Hawk)

Matthew Wills
November 20, 2024
Tarantula hawk wasps offer some of the most painful stings known to humans, giving them almost absolute protection from vertebrate predators.

Insects That Changed History

How the Soviet Union Turned a Plague into Propaganda

Jess Romeo
August 9, 2020
The fight against locust swarms allowed the Soviet Union to consolidate power over neighboring regions.

The Long-Lost Locust

Matthew Wills
June 14, 2018
The 1874 locust swarm was estimated to be twice the square mileage of the state of Colorado. Why don't locusts swarm anymore?

Historical Bugs: Archaeoentomology

Matthew Wills
January 23, 2023
The remains of ancient insects reveal new information about Paleo-Eskimo life and the history of the Norse in Greenland, Iceland, and the Faroe Islands.

How “Termites of the Sea” Have Shaped Maritime Technology

Sierra Garcia
December 24, 2021
These small marine pests have been eating our ships for millennia, forcing us to keep building better boats throughout history.

Insects in the Mail

Danny Robb
December 28, 2024
The efficiency of the postal system and generosity of local experts played important roles in the advancement of entomology in eighteenth-century France.

Bugs and Culture

Insect Jewelry of the Victorian Era

Amelia Soth
January 16, 2020
The wing-cases of gold-enameled weevils hung from necklaces; muslin gowns were embroidered with the iridescent green elytra of jewel beetles.

The War on Bugs

Salama Udaipurwala
October 30, 2024
In the 1950s, supersized insects were the villains in a rash of big-screen horror movies. What did those monstrous roaches represent, and how were they vanquished?

Katrina Gulliver

How did an oleoresin produced by insects in Asia become a standard part of European furniture manufacture and conservation?

The complicated, ever-changing, millennia-long relationship between insects and humans.

Margaret S. Collins, Pioneering Black Entomologist

She was the first African American woman to earn a PhD in entomology as well as an activist for freedom in the Civil Rights Movement.

Could these blood-sucking pests actually have the munchies?

items.title: The Cassette Tapes of the Great Migration
items.description:
An archive of recorded interviews captures how ordinary people experienced one of the defining chapters of American history.

The post The Cassette Tapes of the Great Migration appeared first on JSTOR Daily.
items.content:
In the fall of 1975, Johnetta Brazzell, a young Black woman in a smart plaid blazer, stood inside a small grocery store on the south side of Pontiac, Michigan. She was there to interview the shop owner, T.C. Holland, whose son had been appointed as the city’s first Black mayor the previous year. But Brazzell was not interested in discussing the contemporary politics of the city: an uneasy mix of economic uncertainty as the region’s automotive sector faltered, ongoing racial tensions stemming from school desegregation efforts, and the boisterous civic boosterism that accompanied the debut of Pontiac’s massive new stadium, which locals had nicknamed the Silverdome.

Instead, Brazzell wanted to know how the story had started for the city’s Black residents, who made up more than a quarter of Pontiac’s booming population. She went back to the beginning: “Where were you born?”

By the 1970s, when Brazzell was asking her questions, many had grown disillusioned with the place where they had once seen nothing but opportunity.

Brazzell and several of her colleagues in the Urban Affairs Center at Oakland University, located just outside the Pontiac city limits, were part of a new movement of oral historians documenting the stories of everyday people in their own voices with the use of newly portable and increasingly affordable cassette recorders. “We’re trying to locate people who lived [in Pontiac] and get eyewitness accounts of what was going on, how people lived, where they worked and, generally, just what life was like for them,” she told the Detroit Free Press in 1975. There was an urgency to her efforts. “If we don’t get it from those individuals, then we can’t get it from anyone else. Oral history is usually considered a supplement to written history, but here oral history is the only account anyone has.”

Over the next several years, the oral historians would record about 80 tapes capturing the history of Pontiac’s Black community, along the way mapping the routes of the Great Migration, which drew 6 million people from the rural South to the cities of the Northeast, Midwest, and West in the early and mid-20th century. Today, 23 of those interviews—in audio form with machine-generated transcripts—have been shared via JSTOR by the Oakland University Archives and Special Collections.

Holland, one of the first interviewees, told Brazzell he was born in northeastern Georgia in the first decade of the Jim Crow era. As a teenager he lathered faces in a barbershop catering to white clientele in Atlanta. In his interview, he tried to gloss over the racism he experienced there: “Then sometimes a customer would become dissatisfied by certain things and he’d say certain things and I decided I didn’t want to be bothered with it.” He wasn’t yet 17 when he “had become dissatisfied with the South.” He planned to leave for New York, until a chance encounter with an old neighbor who had returned from his home in Pontiac to move his mother north. Holland joined the family on the ride back to Michigan.

Pontiac, Michigan, had been a town of 10,000 at the turn of the century when Mary and John Morton brought their infant daughter, Nelly, to the city from Canada. In her conversation with Brazzell in 1975, Nelly, who went by her married name, Ryder, did not know how her family had come to settle in Chatham Township in Ontario—then known as the Black Mecca of Canada—nor why they had moved to Pontiac. “Perhaps working conditions were better,” she speculated. With her parents’ encouragement, Ryder would become the first Black student to graduate from the city high school in 1917.

By the time Holland arrived in Pontiac on January 3, 1919, there were more than two-and-a-half times that many people in the city. By 1930, the city’s population would double again. Among the new arrivals in the 1920s were Edith Richardson, who had also lived in Chatham Township before relocating; Adele Walker, who was raised by her grandparents—both formerly enslaved—on a farm in Mississippi, and Mary Belle Scott, who had made her way from Mississippi to East St. Louis (where she witnessed the 1917 massacre that displaced 6,000 Black people) and then to Chicago and Milwaukee before settling in Pontiac.

Scott would become a prominent figure in the Black neighborhood that developed in the southwest of the city. Known to the interviewees as Mellow Lane or Bagley and Wesson—for the intersection that was so central to community life it was referred to simply as “the corner”—the area was home to such institutions as the Newman A.M.E. church, which Scott attended; the Southwest Community Center, where she was a supervisor; and the Bethune Art and Study Club, which Scott and Ryder helped to establish in 1928. “Everybody who’s been here any time knows Mrs. Scott,” Scott remembered people saying.

Black residents continued to arrive through the 1940s, often for jobs at General Motors or Wilson Foundry. Like those who came before them, most settled in the south of the city, in vibrant Black communities that struggled economically after being redlined by the federal government in 1937. But by the 1970s, when Brazzell was asking her questions, many had grown disillusioned with the place where they had once seen nothing but opportunity. “Pontiac is not the Pontiac I used to know,” said Willie Hilton Dean, who had traveled to the city for a two-week visit to his wife’s family in the 1940s and never left. Walker had come to realize that “segregation and all those things are still here, plentiful, but they use different names.”

“Would you like to speculate on the future of Pontiac and what’s gonna happen here?” Brazzell asked as she finished her nearly two-hour conversation at Holland’s Grocery in the fall of 1975. T.C. Holland demurred—“Oh no, I couldn’t, I wouldn’t exactly speculate…”—before declaring himself an optimist.

The city faced a challenging moment—and there would be much more adversity to come in Pontiac—but “crisis brings men together. And when it brings men together, you plot a new course. He may stray from you later, but you and him will walk side by side for a while in that new course,” Holland said. “We walk side by side.”

  • After listening to one or two of the interview recordings, what does hearing the speakers—their pauses, laughter, hesitations, or emotion—add to your understanding that a transcript alone cannot? How should historians treat those vocal elements as evidence?
  • Several interviewees describe migration as a series of decisions shaped by opportunity, chance encounters, violence, discrimination, and family networks rather than a single dramatic departure from the South. How do these individual stories complicate or deepen familiar narratives of the Great Migration? What larger historical patterns emerge when these personal accounts are considered together?
  • Johnetta Brazzell’s interviews capture memories of the early twentieth century alongside the perspectives of people living through the challenges of the 1970s. How does the historical moment in which the interviews were recorded influence the stories people tell about the past? What questions would you ask if you were conducting a follow-up interview today?

items.title: Reading the Maya with William S. Burroughs
items.description:
Burroughs drew on the leading Maya scholarship of his day, much of which has since been overturned.

The post Reading the Maya with William S. Burroughs appeared first on JSTOR Daily.
items.content:
The writers of the Beat generation adopted ideas and images from cultural traditions ranging from Buddhism to jazz. William S. Burroughs repeatedly turned to another source: the ancient Maya. As independent scholar Paul H. Wild writes, Burroughs drastically reshaped Maya culture for his own purposes, but his stories were grounded in ideas about the civilization that were common in academic circles at the time.

Wild writes that Burroughs had a longstanding interest in archaeology and anthropology, and particularly in hieroglyphics. In 1950, he enrolled in Mexico City College, where he studied anthropology of Classic Maya and Aztec civilizations—two cultures he either conflated or intentionally remixed in some of his later work.

Burroughs was fascinated by the hieroglyphic nature of Maya writing, which he claimed could convey ideas more directly.

Wild notes that it’s unclear how much studying Burroughs did in the 18 months he was enrolled at the Mexican college. During that time, he also indulged in heroin, wrote a version of his first novel, Junky, began a quest to find yagé, also known as ayahuasca, and shot and killed his wife, Joan Vollmer, in what he claimed was either an accident or a party trick gone wrong.

In 1950, the academic study of Maya culture was almost totally dependent on writings by the sixteenth-century friar Diego de Landa, who destroyed the vast majority of Maya codices known to Europeans and wrote up his own observations of the literature. Based on Landa’s work, Mayanists of the 1930s and ‘40s developed an image of the classic Maya as a civilization without war, but living under the control of astronomer-priests who used their complex calendars to rule the common people.

In Burroughs’ 1961 novel The Soft Machine, Maya priests use a “control machine” to telepathically enslave the common people until a time-traveler destroys the machine, leading to a revolt.

More to Explore

How the Beat Generation Became “Beatniks”

Matthew Wills
May 5, 2019
The rebellious culture of the Beat Generation was coopted into fodder for a marketable lifestyle.

Wild writes that, somewhat paradoxically, given his profession, Burroughs railed against the “Word Virus” as a tool of control. And so he was fascinated by the hieroglyphic nature of Maya writing, which he claimed could convey ideas more directly, avoiding the need for words. This followed a common scholarly notion that Maya hieroglyphics were not tied to spoken language.

Many of the ideas about Maya life that Burroughs had access to in the 1950s were turned on their head in the next decade, when epigraphers realized that Maya writing was, in fact, partly phonological, and could be directly translated into speech.

This field is for validation purposes and should be left unchanged.

Get your fix of JSTOR Daily’s best stories in your inbox each Thursday.

This led to a breakthrough in translation, which, along with new archaeological discoveries, produced new understandings. For instance, classic-period images that had been understood to represent the priestly class actually showed rulers and warriors—and it turned out that the Maya had engaged in plenty of warfare. By 1999, the general view was that there were no priests in classic Maya communities, and that they only appeared in the Postclassic Maya revival in the northern Yucatan starting around 1000 CE—the period of the materials Landa had access to.

Of course, given the loose relationship between scholarship and Burroughs’ uses of it, all that may be beside the point for anyone reading his novels.

items.title: What Happened to the Bones of the American Bison?
items.description:
The near-extinction of the bison sparked an industry that left almost nothing of the animals behind.

The post What Happened to the Bones of the American Bison? appeared first on JSTOR Daily.
items.content:
The mass slaughter of the American bison during the 1870s and 1880s was unprecedented. The shaggy bovines of the plains and boreal forests were nearly hunted to extinction in a frenzy of killing that decimated their population. There were tens of millions at the beginning of the century, and barely a few hundred by 1890.

The animals were killed for their hides and their tongues, a culinary delicacy, but also as part of the campaign to ethnically cleanse Native Americans from the land. The John Wayne character in the quintessential movie of settler-colonialism, The Searchers (1956), makes the connection outright: no bison, no food for the Comanche in winter. Bison slaughter was a form of biocide in service of genocide, although neither ultimately achieved its aims.

Historian Casey Pallister argues that the brief but intense era of the bone hunters, those who scoured the land for the bones, should be better known.

Less well known is that the vast numbers of bones left over didn’t just sit there to decompose over time. They fueled a brief but intensive extractive industry that lasted as long as the raw material. An infamous image of a mountain of bison skulls tells the story in the small print of the caption: they are piled up outside Detroit’s Michigan Carbon Works plant. The bones were the raw material for factories.

The bones were ground up into bone ash, used as fertilizer, and burned to make bone black, used both as a dye and a filter for cane sugar juice. Michigan Carbon’s “Homestead Guano,” for example, was famous on farms to the south and east; belying the name, it wasn’t bird excrement but ground-up bison bones. Meanwhile, remaining hides, skulls, and hoofs could be made into glue. A smaller amount of the bone was turned into buttons, knife handles, fans, and umbrella ribs, bone being a cheap substitute for ivory before the age of plastic.

Historian Casey Pallister argues that the brief but intense era of the bone hunters, those who scoured the land for the bones, should be better known:

The carcasses of the great animals, picked clean by scavengers and left to bleach in the prairie sun, proved immensely important as sources of labor, capital, survival, and imagination in the North American West.

The bison bone trade “was part of a web of well-organized capitalist extraction industries” in which bone hunters were “part of a laboring class as much as they were opportunistic individuals looking to make an extra dollar.”

More to Explore

Where the Bison Roam—Again?

Matthew Wills
March 28, 2020
The American bison isn't extinct. But could it ever roam freely across North America, as it once did? Some scholars say it could happen.

Settler colonialism is characterized in part by the erasure of the history of those removed and replaced, so American myth tells of bootstrapping settlers exploiting the bones. But, as Pallister notes, “when one examines primary literature, it is apparent that Native Americans undoubtedly dominated the workforce, carving out their own place in the prairie industry but often doing so for similar reasons as most white settlers: survival.”

Barred from jobs outside wage labor, Native Americans sometimes “exercised considerable power over the price per ton of bones because of the dependency of middlemen on their labors.” Mixed-ancestry people (called Métis in Canada) who were not bound to reservations, in particular, roamed far and wide collecting bones and came to dominate the trade. As Pallister writes, “The bone trade proved part of a continuous pursuit of bison bodies for sustenance as well as trade goods in the American capitalist system.” It was “hardly a replacement for the rich bison-hunting lifestyle of the past,” but it “at times revealed a certain level of cultural continuity.”

Bones from about one hundred complete skeletons made up a ton of weight, which earned bone-hunters $4-$12, depending on the market. (Edwin Ford Piper has “a dollar for a ton” in his poem “Dry Bones,” quoted by Pallister.) The work was hard, and a gamble: “one might hit the ‘motherlode’ and accumulate considerable weight in a matter of hours, but more often it took days and long distances to fill a wagon or cart.”

The bone boom lasted less than two decades, and, being self-devouring, left little trace on the landscape. It was a kind of double erasure: no animals, no remains. Yet there are still hints: before being named for Queen Victoria, Regina, the capital of Saskatchewan, was known as Pile-of-Bones because it was a staging point for bison bone.

items.title: How Sir Lawrence Alma-Tadema Imagined Ancient Rome
items.description:
The Victorian painter drew on archaeology and ancient texts to create richly detailed scenes of love and excess.

The post How Sir Lawrence Alma-Tadema Imagined Ancient Rome appeared first on JSTOR Daily.
items.content:
A healthy portion of Sir Lawrence Alma-Tadema’s artworks recreates life in ancient Rome. Forget about military might, imperialism, and portrayals of heroic feats, though. His Rome is very much a hedonistic society. Through his paintings, “We are to be fascinated by the idle rich at their leisure, to delight with the revellers who carouse and the lovers who make love, and to marvel at the magnificence, opulence, and utter decadence,” writes Rosemary Barrow in Bulletin of the Institute of Classical Studies.

While his contemporaries indulged in Medieval-inspired imagery in their paintings, Sir Lawrence Alma-Tadema was more interested in depictions of Classical antiquity. “On an initial reading, many paintings appear little more than gorgeous depictions of marble, flowers, and Mediterranean sunlight, until we decipher the imagery, which invariably subverts apparent meaning,” writes Barrow.

Alma-Tadema imported roses from the French Riviera to ensure a continual fresh supply while actively working on the painting.

Alma-Tadema also looked to historical, archaeological, and literary evidence for inspiration. In the realm of literature, “The texts chosen by Alma-Tadema are much the same as those employed by other British classical-subject painters: they are drawn from the witty, urbane, and carefree world of Latin love poetry: the poems of Catullus, the elegies of Tibullus, Propertius, and Ovid, and the Odes of Horace.” Catullus and Lesbia are frequent subjects of Alma-Tadema’s, as are Tibullus and his beloved Delia.

According to Barrow, the first British painting to seek inspiration from Latin love poetry is Alma-Tadema’s Catullus at Lesbia’s of 1865, painted three years after Ludwig Schwabe’s influential biography of the poet, which surmised that Lesbia was the cultured, refined, and married aristocrat Clodia Metelli. “Lesbia’s house is portrayed as a richly decorated Pompeian interior, cluttered with expensive gold and silver plates and statuary, which, in addition to being decorative, serve to emphasize her wealth and status,” writes Barrow. A wall painting depicts a satyr anticipating copulation with a goat. “This is the most sexually explicit image ever used by any nineteenth-century British classical-subject painter.”

When it comes to archaeological sources, Spring depicts a procession headed by angelic flower girls winding its way through the marble-lined streets of imperial Rome. The occasion is the April Floralia, sacred to Flora, the ancient Italian goddess of flowers, vegetation, and fertility. “The painting presents a wealth of archaeological details: the roundels of the banner and tympana carried by the celebrants are decorated with paintings of semi-nude frolicking couples,” writes Barrow. “The roundel figures imitate nymphs and satyrs from a wall painting in the House of the Dioscuri, at Pompeii, while the tympana paintings imitate those from the House of the Vettii at Pompeii, excavated in 1894, the very year the painting was completed.”

Architectural and statuary elements aside, roses in particular bear a special significance in Alma-Tadema’s depiction of Roman life: he depicts women smelling roses; roses being presented as gifts; and roses also appear in the titles of his paintings. For Victorian audiences, this was a familiar motif. “The usual nineteenth-century association for roses was with beautiful girls and with sensuous love,” writes Barrow. Alma-Tadema, however, also sought to incorporate roses into his paintings with a focus on their significance in the Roman world.

“For Alma-Tadema, roses mean love and revelry, but they also carry with them a distinctive Roman aura of excess,” Barrow says. Consider paintings like Caracalla, where the titular emperor treads a trail of rose petals; or In a Rose Garden, where a woman shakes the petals of a rose bush down on her companion; and the extravaganza of The Roses of Heliogabalus. “It was Athenaeus’ Cleopatra who once gave a banquet at which the guests were knee-deep in rose petals; Suetonius’ Nero who once demanded that a courtier spend over four million sesterces on roses for a dinner party in his honor; Tacitus’ Vitellius who visited a grisly battlefield after his path was strewn with rose petals.”

More to Explore

Bread, Circuses, Baths: Bathing in Rome, the Public Way

Matthew Wills
December 8, 2025
By the fourth century CE, Rome had some 856 privately owned public baths, the grounds of which served as civic gardens adorned with sculptures.

History, literature, and archaeology all coalesce in Alma-Tadema’s painting The Roses of Heliogabalus, which depicts a little-known episode from the Historia Augusta: “In a banqueting-room with a reversible ceiling Heliogabalus once overwhelmed his parasites with violets and other flowers, so that some of them were actually smothered to death, being unable to crawl out to the top.”

This field is for validation purposes and should be left unchanged.

Get your fix of JSTOR Daily’s best stories in your inbox each Thursday.

The emperor is wearing a tunic of silk and gold thread, while his dining couches are inlaid with silver and mother-of-pearl. “Other details are based on archaeological artefacts and, as usual, Alma-Tadema’s use of archaeology is not arbitrary, but contributes to the scene,” says Barrow. “In the background stands a bronze statue of Bacchus, faun, and panther, copied from an actual marble group in the Vatican Museums.”

The voluptuousness of the atmosphere evokes a mood of nineteenth-century literary decadence. “Théophile Gautier bitterly regrets that the richness of the antique world cannot be recaptured by the modern imagination and laments not having been a contemporary of Sardanapalus […] Heliogabalus, while Joris-Karl Huysmans describes Heliogabalus as treading in silver dust and sand of gold, his head crowned with a tiara and his clothes studded with jewels.”

The decadence extends beyond the subject matter: Alma-Tadema imported roses from the French Riviera to ensure a continual fresh supply while actively working on the painting.

Oddly, though, nobody in The Roses of Heliogabalus is smelling the roses. “His interest in Rome, ultimately, is vested in its corruption, luxury, and sensuality, and yet his access to all of this extravagance is essentially intellectual and conceptual,” concludes Barrow. This tension and paradox ultimately give his paintings a depth that the shiny textures and surfaces he portrays might, at first, conceal in the name of aestheticism.

items.title: The Debate Over Pictures in Science
items.description:
Botanical illustrations helped bring science to new audiences—but not every scientist welcomed the change.

The post The Debate Over Pictures in Science appeared first on JSTOR Daily.
items.content:
In 1843, English botanist Joseph Hooker returned from Antarctica with samples and illustrations of plants from his expedition. But when he found a publisher, he was distressed that they did not have the right priorities. He wrote that the publisher “cares nought for my descriptions at all, & would not care a straw whether all the plants were European or Antarctic.”

People bought these books primarily for the pictures. Advances in printing technologies had enabled a new type of popular science built around mass-produced illustrations. Historian Anne Secord argues that while some botanists saw these images as an important tool in a “quest to expand the scientific community,” others saw danger.

For some, images produced the wrong type of pleasure, distracting from real learning.

Making new botanists was a real problem. Secord writes that nineteenth century botanists “constantly lamented the small number of practitioners and stressed the need to sustain popular interest in the science in the hope of encouraging wider participation.”

Then the 1815 Apothecaries’ Act in Britain required doctors to learn botany, and the demand for lectures surged, among both students and interested outsiders. Secord writes that this gave a wider audience access to botanical illustrations. She quotes William Hooker, Joseph’s father, who lectured at the University of Glasgow. “I could have done nothing but for the illustrations,” he wrote. “Nothing could exceed the interest shown by that Class:—in short they came for the pleasure of the thing.”

But were they going to become effective botanists—or even botanists at all? Scientists disagreed about both questions. Secord argues that the controversy centered on the nature of pleasure.

Scientists struggled to find a balance between the pleasures of the eye and those of the mind. Secord writes that astronomer John Herschel “contrasted the ‘easy access’ of those ‘who cater for the passions’ with the difficulties experienced by promoters of ‘sound knowledge or rational instruction.’”

More to Explore

The Metamorphosis of a 17th-Century Insect Artist

Allison C. Meier
December 24, 2018
Maria Sibylla Merian's work in the natural sciences was overlooked for centuries. Now a rare butterfly has been named in her honor.

For some, images produced the wrong type of pleasure, distracting from real learning. Naturalists like Peter Rylands believed that written descriptions would prevent unserious people from taking up the science, and would make better practitioners.

But others believed images were the key to botany’s future. Secord explains that Edwin Lees likened “Rylands’s objections … to rejecting a candle at dusk or refusing to use a guide in an unknown country.” There was “no talismanic power in scientific language,” Lees wrote, and he argued that images allowed the eye and mind to work together in a way that words could not.

Weekly Newsletter

"*" indicates required fields

This field is for validation purposes and should be left unchanged.

Get your fix of JSTOR Daily’s best stories in your inbox each Thursday.

Lees was careful to argue that images should be grounded in expertise. Herschel agreed, saying that images could be a good hook, but that pleasure “should not be a mere ‘cloak for the instruction intended to be conveyed.’”

Images had additional potential in disciplines like anatomy, where specimens were more difficult to obtain. For medical students, practicing with real cadavers would remain important. But lecturers increasingly used images to bring new groups of people into science.

Secord believes these episodes should bring us “a greater awareness of the inclusionist aims of expert practitioners, which were inscribed in the ways in which they promoted their science.”

items.title: Life Inside Icelandic Turf Houses
items.description:
Grass roofs may look enchanting today, but living beneath them was another story.

The post Life Inside Icelandic Turf Houses appeared first on JSTOR Daily.
items.content:
Let’s tour an Icelandic turf house. From the side, you could be forgiven for mistaking it for a hill; a thick carpet of grass grows up the walls and over the roof. But look closer and you can see a little windowpane peering out from behind the dandelions, and around the side there is a house-front and a door leading into a dark passageway.

Inside, a hallway paved with flat stones and packed earth opens on one side to the kitchen, with its stone hearth and huge iron pots; above, strings of fish hang to dry in the smoke. On the other side is the pantry, with butter churns and great tubs of skyr.

During the bitterest cold, sheep might be brought in to the lower level of the house, so that their body heat would bring just a little more warmth to the home.

Up a steep little staircase you’ll find a long lofted room known as the baðstofa, where everyone except the master and mistress of the house crams together to sleep, two to a narrow bed. And by everyone, I mean everyone—not just the children, but also grandparents, servants, and local “paupers”—widows, orphans, or people with disabilities who were placed with the family as household help.

The baðstofa was the center of household life. Here, the household ate together, sitting on their beds, and whiled away the dark winter days by spinning, weaving, telling stories, reciting poems, and playing chess. During the bitterest cold, sheep might be brought in to the lower level of the house, so that their body heat would bring just a little more warmth to the home.

To be clear, this is a depiction of a relatively well-to-do turf house. A more humble dwelling is described by archaeologist Kristján Mímisson in Building Identities: The Architecture of the Persona. This house, built for a single hermit, had only one roof-post, and consequently only one room tall enough to stand in; the passageways were so narrow that Mímisson likens them to “squeezing through a cave fissure,” and the entrance to one room was so low that it could only be entered by crawling.

More to Explore

On the Anniversary of Iceland’s Independence

S. N. Johnson-Roehr
June 17, 2024
Iceland is celebrating its 80th anniversary. Three photograph collections shared on JSTOR show how much has—and hasn’t—changed on the island since independence.

Turf houses were an ingenious response to scarcity. For centuries, the only wood suitable for building houses on the island was the driftwood that washed up from shipwrecks and distant forests. As a result, Icelandic house-plans had to use a minimum of wood—just a few posts and roof beams. The rest of the structure was made from stones (carefully stacked, with no mortar) and turf cut into chunks from the peat bogs. If done just right, the turf would grow together and form a cohesive, insulating layer.

What was it really like to live in a turf house? Visitors at the time did not mince words. This account comes from Sir George Steuart Mackenzie’s Travels in Iceland:

The thick turf walls, the earthen floors kept continually damp and filthy, the personal uncleanliness of the inhabitants, all unite in causing a smell insupportable to a stranger… There is no mode of ventilating any part of the house; and as twenty people sometimes eat and sleep in the same apartment, very pungent vapours are added in no small quantity, to the plentiful effluvia proceeding from fish, bags of oil, skins, &c. A farm house looks more like a village than a single habitation. Sometimes several families live enclosed within the same mass of turf.

Mackenzie writes with the characteristic judgmental sniff of an upper-crust tourist. Icelanders themselves, however, seem to have abandoned the turf house with enthusiasm, just as soon as there were alternatives. Before 1910, the majority of the country lived in turf houses. By the 1930s, stone and concrete had overtaken turf, and today, the few that remain have mostly been converted to museums.

"*" indicates required fields

This field is for validation purposes and should be left unchanged.

Get your fix of JSTOR Daily’s best stories in your inbox each Thursday.

But abandoning the turf house wasn’t just a matter of comfort and convenience. Until 1944, Iceland was under Danish rule. As the nationalist movement in Iceland gained momentum beginning in the 1700s, nationalist activists felt pressure to prove that Iceland was mature enough to rule itself.

In “Icelandic Putridity”: Colonial Thought and Icelandic Architectural Heritage, Sigurjón Baldur Hafsteinsson explores how this dynamic manifested itself in a rejection of turf houses. Hafsteinsson quotes the Icelandic nationalist Sigurður Guðmundsson, writing in 1860:

It is imperative that we liberate ourselves from the foreign perception which holds that we have always remained defenseless weaklings, lacking the means to survive, and we had nothing but mud-huts to crawl into like barbarians.

Even though, according to Guðmundsson, Danish architecture wasn’t really better—he described it as “houses mostly made from half-baked bricks, piled on top of one another in a makeshift way”—the turf house had become a symbol of “backwardness,” something to be left behind as Iceland modernized.

Today, when you look up “turf houses,” you’ll find article after article celebrating them as “green design,” “eco-friendly,” and “sustainable.” The Icelanders of the nationalist movement saw turf houses through the lens of their struggle for independence from Denmark; today, we see them through the lens of a different anxiety—our distance from nature and our impact on the environment. It’s striking how perspectives change.

* * *

For the Classroom

  • A turf house can look charming today, but the sources in this article tell a more complicated story. How do the meanings of these homes change across time, and what drives those changes?
  • The story draws on archaeologists, travelers, and Icelandic nationalists. How does each perspective shape your understanding of turf houses?
  • Turf houses have been seen as symbols of poverty, national identity, and sustainability. What does this tell us about the way successive generations reinterpret the past?
  • How does the story of the turf house complicate the idea that “progress” means leaving the past behind?

items.title: What Was Sewer Socialism?
items.description:
Milwaukee mayor Daniel Hoan believed the best argument for socialism was a city government that worked.

The post What Was Sewer Socialism? appeared first on JSTOR Daily.
items.content:
Recent victories for democratic socialist politicians like Zohran Mamdani in New York and Janeese Lewis George in Washington, DC have gotten a lot of people talking about the “sewer socialists” who came to power in the 1910s Midwest, especially in Milwaukee. Historian Michael E. Stevens looks at how one such politician, Daniel Webster Hoan Jr., applied big ideological principles to the daily grind of running a city.

In the early 1900s, Stevens writes, political corruption and graft was a notorious problem in Milwaukee. The local Socialist Party vowed to take this issue on, running a slate of candidates in 1910 on the promise of addressing issues like no-bid contracts. The plan worked. Emile Seidel, who would later go on to be Eugene V. Debs’ running mate in the 1912 presidential election, became mayor. His party also won 21 out of 35 seats on the Common Council. And Hoan was elected city attorney.

Hoan framed socialism as an extension of existing public institutions like the post office, schools, parks, roads, and museums.

Over the years that followed, Hoan fought the city utility and street railway companies, winning reductions in fees and improvements in service. In 1916, he was elected mayor, a job he would hold for the next 24 years.

Stevens writes that Hoan framed socialism as an extension of existing public institutions like the post office, schools, parks, roads, and museums. In his view, other important institutions like railroads, factories, and banks should be run in the same fashion. For that argument to work, he believed, government had to run efficiently and without corruption. He spoke out strongly against the idea that lower taxes were needed. Instead, he prioritized a fairer tax structure and government programs that directly helped everyone in the city.

More to Explore

A Million Americans Once Voted for an Incarcerated Socialist

Morgan Godvin
April 21, 2023
Eugene Debs campaigned for both president and prison reform from a federal penitentiary. His critiques of the prison system still resonate.

His initial priorities as mayor included vaccinations, clean drinking water, improvements to the city’s harbor, and city planning. In 1920, Milwaukee became the twelfth city in the country to adopt a comprehensive zoning ordinance.

Instead of relying solely on hiring firefighters, he also used the municipality’s power for fire prevention and housing improvements. His efforts to reduce crime included not just fighting graft in the police department but also offering more recreational activities.

Weekly Newsletter

"*" indicates required fields

This field is for validation purposes and should be left unchanged.

Get your fix of JSTOR Daily’s best stories in your inbox each Thursday.

During World War I, Stevens writes, Hoan resisted profiteering by purchasing surplus material—including salt, canned peas, shoes, and blankets—from the U.S. Army and selling them through city offices. At a time of high inflation, he was able to charge less than half the normal retail price. He argued that this “should demonstrate once and for all that the Socialist theory in conducting many of our enterprises without profits can be worked out in a grand and beneficial manner.”

In 1936, Time magazine called Hoan a “Marxist Mayor” but praised the good schools and low crime rate he had helped achieve.

In 1940, Hoan was finally defeated, by a political newcomer known for singing “God Bless America” at his rallies and making vague promises of bringing jobs to the city. By that time, though, many of the ideas Hoan had championed had made their way into the Democratic Party in the proudly pro-government New Deal.

items.title: The Rise and Fall of the Public Sandbox
items.description:
A nineteenth-century experiment in children's play helped reshape American cities—and later fell out of favor.

The post The Rise and Fall of the Public Sandbox appeared first on JSTOR Daily.
items.content:
Playing in the sand is probably as old as the first humanoids to wander onto a beach. But bringing sand indoors for children to play with appears to have been an innovation of the nineteenth-century German kindergarten movement. From there it moved outdoors, to sand piles, sand hills, and sand gardens, culminating in the readily-contained sandbox, which could be set up anywhere.

As scholar Tamar Zinguer details, women brought the sandbox to the US in the 1880s and made it public as a women-centered space in an era when there were very few such spaces.

The sandbox was a space where “an attitude of respect, collegiality and participation prevailed, in a rare place with universal appeal.”

“Women doctors, benefactors, women educators, and mothers took part in this experiment to claim a public space for working mothers and children in city life. The sandbox, considered to be the direct precursor of the play-ground, built communities through play.”

During an 1884 trip to Germany, Boston physician Marie Zakrzewska, one of the very few women doctors in the US, witnessed children having a whale of a time on the sand hills in Berlin’s parks. She wrote home with the news. Alongside the Massachusetts Emergency and Hygiene Association (MEHA), an offshoot of the Boston Woman’s Education Association, Zakrzewska was instrumental in establishing sand play in Boston. German women who had trained as kindergartners and then immigrated to the US helped spread the sand around elsewhere in the US.

Zinguer calls sand play “‘tacit’ knowledge, requiring no explanation or special understanding.” The sandbox was a space where “an attitude of respect, collegiality and participation prevailed, in a rare place with universal appeal.”

Pioneering psychologist G. Stanley Hall—he would later be noted as the only American university president to invite Sigmund Freud to lecture in the US—disagreed. Regardless of the emerging reality in Boston, his 1888 study of two boys at play in the sand argued that girls should be excluded from such play: “Most destructive in the ‘sand-pile’ are little girls, who quite fail to appreciate it.”

Disregarding the patriarchal voice of academia, Boston already had 17 MEHA-run playgrounds with sandboxes before the city opened its first public playground in a city park. This was Charlesbank, which opened in 1891 and was designed by Frederick Law Olmsted as a satellite to his Emerald Necklace chain of parks in Boston and Brookline. Charlesbank included a “sand court” run (and funded) by an all-women committee, rather than the all-male parks commission. It also hosted a women’s and men’s open-air gymnasia, with a running track around the men’s gymnasium, a design that would prove highly influential. (The women’s gymnasium and the sand court were surrounded by tall hedges.)

More to Explore

Changing Playground Design, Changing How Children Play

Laura Clawson
August 13, 2025
The built environment of the playground influences children’s play styles, and even small interventions can affect cognitive and social-emotional development.

The apotheosis of the sandbox was probably its inclusion in the 1904 World’s Fair in St. Louis, which helped put sandboxes on the world’s map. The sandboxes at the Fair were part of the Model Playground in the Model Street exhibit, which also included a “town hall, a municipal museum, an emergency hospital and drugstore.”

“The Model Playground, occupying three quarters of an acre, was considered the more modest of these exhibits, yet the most successful,” writes Zinguer. The matron-supervised playground acted as a nursery, day care center, and “lost children” collection point for the over 1,000 kids who misplaced their parents over the run of the fair. “Native” children, among the 3000-strong indigenous peoples on exhibit from around the world, were also included in sandy playtime.

“Increasingly recognized as a ‘community builder’ throughout the beginning of the 20th century, a sandbox appeared to imply ‘normalcy,’ if only by allowing children to play freely and be engrossed in their own alternative reality.”

Sandbox use continued through the mid-century, but the tide turned later in the twentieth century. Once celebrated as sites of creative play, sandboxes came to be “considered a breeder of disease and infestation.” This is because sandboxes can become infected with fecal microbes and parasites from wild and domesticated animals—including millions of free-roaming cats.

While sandboxes haven’t disappeared, they have become hard to find, and public ones, the whole point of the original sandbox, now seem largely a thing of the past.

items.title: The Meaning Behind Philippine Crucifixions
items.description:
An anthropologist examines the sacred vows that inspire some Filipino Catholics to reenact Christ's Passion each Holy Week.

The post The Meaning Behind Philippine Crucifixions appeared first on JSTOR Daily.
items.content:
Does signing up to be crucified take ethnography too far? Anthropologist Julius Bautista once had to confront this unexpected question while doing fieldwork in Cutud, San Fernando.

This barangay or district in provincial Pampanga is home to perhaps the most spectacular commemoration of Good Friday in the Philippines. There, devotees annually re-enact Christianity’s holiest week in an amateur performance that culminates with the crucifixion of some participants. The tradition was introduced in Cutud in the mid-twentieth century, but was thrust into the spotlight when televised by the media in the 1980s.

When the director of a passion play offered to nail Bautista to a cross in the name of empirical authenticity, the anthropologist declined.

Theater scholars Anril Pineda Tiatco and Amihan Bonifacio-Ramolete trace Holy Week performances (sinakulo) to European “passion plays” about the death of Christ. Self-mortifying pamagdarame rituals, including whipping and crucifixion, likewise have roots in medieval Christian tradition.

Those traditions became more than an object of study when Bautista was invited to take part himself. When the director of a passion play offered to nail Bautista to a cross in the name of empirical authenticity, the anthropologist declined.

“Although I was brought up Catholic, I did not have any specific religious motivations for pursuing nailing,” Bautista reflects. “[W]ithout those religious motivations, I would not be engaging in the same act that I was attempting to understand.”

Key to this practice of crucifixion is a vow called a panata, which Bautista describes as “a divine transaction… for which self-mortification would be the reciprocal act.”

The anguish that devotees experience during crucifixion “is seen in the light of sacrifice and is associated with panata as a contract” with God, explain Tiatco and Bonifacio-Ramolete.

As some participants vow to be crucified in exchange for family members’ recovery from ill health, panata is also understood as a sacrifice made out of love for others in the community. Such faith can help to sustain residents of Cutud, where poverty and hardship are common.

More to Explore

A Christian Case for Gossip

Livia Gershon
March 26, 2026
When silence allows harm to continue, warning others may become a difficult but necessary moral choice.

Participants take panata so seriously that the play’s director initially refused to permit a 40-year-old welder who had spent his life savings traveling to Cutud to be crucified.

The man claimed that “he was committed to absolving himself of a grave sin, which he refused to reveal,” Bautista recounts. But the director insisted that crucifixion “was not based on atoning for sinfulness but… a promise of vow fulfillment or thanksgiving.”

Bautista also quotes the director’s admonition: “I will only allow him to be nailed if he can show me that he understands what panata means.”

In other parts of the country, Holy Week penitents may fulfill their vows in different forms. On the island of Marinduque, local men express panata by performing in the sinakulo as elaborately costumed Roman centurions called morions. Heavy masks, worn to preserve morions’ traditional anonymity, contribute to their discomfort. As one scholar observes, “Presumably the pain provides penitents with greater empathy for the sufferings of Christ.”

Meanwhile, Catholics in a small barangay in lowland Bicol center their worship on the Amang Hinulid. This term, meaning “the father who is laid out in death,” refers to a wooden figure of the “dead” Christ, which is venerated in a ritual funeral on Good Friday. Some devotees cured of illness vow to stage a days-long passion play or tanggal in the Ama’s honor.

In fact, Tiatco and Bonifacio-Ramolete note that “[e]very Catholic community in the Philippines has its own version” of sinakulo. But they aren’t always bound by panata.

For example, nailing is also carried out in the village of Kapitangan, in Bulacan province, where it emerged after the crucifixion of a teenage girl in the late 1970s. Unlike in Cutud, participants are mostly female faith healers adhering not to vows but to mystic trances and possession.

Here, “the ritual serves as an instrument of empowerment” that “demonstrate[s] the intimate relationship” between faith healers and God to their own followers, explains Peter Bräunlein.

In contrast with popular narratives about “the peculiarity of Philippine crucifixion and its bizarre, exotic aura,” Bräunlein argues that Filipino Catholics identify themselves as Christian through “literal interpretation of the ‘founding myth’” of their religion: the Passion of Christ.

items.title: Six Stories with First-Person Narrators
items.description:
Distinctive voices and unforgettable perspectives, by Danielle Evans, Jamil Jan Kochai, Catherine Niu, Thomas Bernhard, Christine Schutt, and Michael Deagler.

The post Six Stories with First-Person Narrators appeared first on JSTOR Daily.
items.content:
When a work of fiction is written in the first person, the story is filtered through the perspective of a single character speaking in the voice of “I,” describing events as they experience them. As the guiding consciousness of a narrative, the first-person voice is a remarkably flexible instrument: narrators range from the selfless to the self-absorbed, from the avoidant to the obsessive, from the wisecracking to the earnest. In these six selections, the way each story is told is crucial to understanding who the narrator is—and what the story is really about. As always, all are free to download.

“Alcatraz” by Danielle Evans
Danielle Evans’ narrator is observant, warm, and determined to reunite her mother with her estranged family during a tour of Alcatraz. The story is as much about the narrator’s desire for family as it is about her mother’s. As she poignantly observes, “You take nothing for granted when the price of it is etched across the face of the person you love the most, when you are born into a series of debts and know you will never be up to the cost of the loan.”

“Hungry Ricky Daddy” by Jamil Jan Kochai
In “Hungry Ricky Daddy,” the narrator tells the story of his friend Ricky Daddy and his love for activist Nabeela, and how falling in love spurs the friend to begin a hunger strike. With humor and charm, the narrator recounts Ricky Daddy’s misadventures in love, until the narrative begins to shift in ways that cast the story in a different light.

More to Explore

Six Flash Fiction Stories by Contemporary Writers

Anna Mebel
May 5, 2026
Compact narratives of precision and surprise, by Lydia Davis, Aimee Bender, Stuart Dybek, Venita Blackburn, and more.

“Chauffeur” by Catherine Niu
In Catherine Niu’s “Chauffeur,” a driver reflects on his childhood, his luck at cards, and the quiet rules of his profession, taking pride in himself as a nondescript presence who tends to disappear in rooms. But a narrator who wants to disappear is still the narrator of his own story, and the story shows us that the chauffeur might yearn for something after all, to deal the cards instead of taking the hand he’s dealt.

“A Testimony” by Thomas Bernhard
Famous for his cranky narrators and long sentences, Thomas Bernhard is a genius at writing obsessive narrators: misanthropes who will never let anything go. In this story, the narrator is supposed to testify that he saw a murderer on a train but instead spends his time railing against the landscape, the train, his fellow passengers, and ultimately, the problems of existence.

“Metropolis” by Christine Schutt
In this terse, elegant story, a mother is confronted by a teacher about her son’s anger problems at school. But the real anger belongs to the narrator herself, who berates herself for bringing a succession of troubled men into her son’s life. As she lies awake beside her son, listening to a dying lover in the next room, she wonders: “does my son hear, is he really sleeping, and how is it I have let this happen to us, opening the door to men who come in or who do not come in …”

“Pat’s, Geno’s” by Michael Deagler
Michael Deagler’s newly sober narrator, Monk, rages against a newly gentrified Philadelphia and attempts to reconnect with an old flame. Monk offers stunning moments of self-insight, or, more often, self-laceration: “I was a man at odds with his surroundings. I was perhaps less bubbly than my usual self.” The pleasure of the story lies in the piercing clarity of Monk’s observations—about Philadelphia, about choosing the right cheesesteak, and about whether it’s possible to start over with a clean slate.
